questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing kwashiorkor with marasmus and jaundice with other disorders of the digestive system by cause and symptoms
questions.question: Two malnourished children are examined. Child P, recently weaned and fed mainly on carbohydrate-rich food, has swollen limbs and abdomen (oedema), thin hair and fat still present under the skin. Child Q, an infant, is extremely wasted with no subcutaneous fat. A third patient, an adult, has yellow skin and eyes. Which comparison is correct?
options: A) P has marasmus caused by deficiency of both proteins and calories; Q has kwashiorkor
B) P and Q both have kwashiorkor; the adult has diarrhoea

C) P has kwashiorkor, caused by protein deficiency when the diet is not short of calories, with wasting of muscles, thinning of hair and oedema while some fat remains; Q has marasmus, caused by simultaneous deficiency of proteins and calories, usually in infants under a year when mother's milk is replaced too early, with emaciation and loss of subcutaneous fat; the adult has jaundice, in which the liver is affected and the skin and eyes turn yellow due to deposition of bile pigments
D) The adult's yellow skin is due to indigestion caused by inadequate enzyme secretion
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) P kwashiorkor (protein deficiency, oedema, fat retained); Q marasmus (protein + calorie deficiency, emaciation); adult jaundice (bile pigments).
Concept: Inflammation of the intestinal tract is the most common ailment due to bacterial or viral infections; infections are also caused by parasites of the intestine like tape worm, round worm, thread worm, hook worm, pin worm, etc. Jaundice: the liver is affected, skin and eyes turn yellow due to the deposit of bile pigments. Vomiting: it is the ejection of stomach contents through the mouth; this reflex action is controlled by the vomit centre in the medulla. Diarrhoea: the abnormal frequency of bowel movement and increased liquidity of the faecal discharge; it reduces the absorption of food. Constipation: the faeces are retained within the colon as the bowel movements occur irregularly. Indigestion: food is not properly digested, leading to a feeling of fullness; causes are inadequate enzyme secretion, anxiety, food poisoning, overeating and spicy food. Protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) may affect large sections of the population during drought, famine and war. Marasmus is produced by a simultaneous deficiency of proteins and calories; it is found in infants less than a year in age if mother's milk is replaced too early by other foods poor in both proteins and caloric value; it leads to impaired growth, replacement of tissue proteins, extreme emaciation of the body and thinning of limbs; the skin becomes dry, thin and wrinkled; growth rate and body weight decline considerably. Kwashiorkor is produced by protein deficiency unaccompanied by calorie deficiency; it results from the replacement of mother's milk by a high-calorie, low-protein diet in a child more than one year in age; like marasmus, it shows wasting of muscles, thinning of limbs, failure of growth and brain development, but unlike marasmus some fat is still left under the skin; moreover, extensive oedema and swelling of body parts are seen.
Why: Calories spare fat stores in kwashiorkor, while the protein shortage lowers plasma proteins and causes oedema; in marasmus both are lacking, so the body consumes its own fat and tissue.
Why not the others: (A) Labels reversed. (B) Q's features are of marasmus; yellow skin indicates jaundice. (D) Indigestion does not deposit bile pigments.
Key point: Kwashiorkor: protein deficiency, oedema, fat retained; marasmus: protein + calorie deficiency, emaciation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting disorders of the muscular and skeletal system by tissue affected and cause, and counting bones in parts of the human skeleton
questions.question: Consider: myasthenia gravis, muscular dystrophy, tetany, arthritis, osteoporosis, gout. How many primarily affect joints, how many are autoimmune, and how many bones are there in the axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs)?
options: A) 3 joint disorders; 2 autoimmune; 126 axial bones
C) 2 (arthritis, gout); 1 autoimmune (myasthenia gravis); 80 axial bones (skull 29 including ear ossicles and hyoid, 26 vertebrae, 1 sternum, 24 ribs)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2 joint disorders; 1 autoimmune; 80 axial bones.
Concept: Myasthenia gravis: auto immune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction, leading to fatigue, weakening and paralysis of skeletal muscle. Muscular dystrophy: progressive degeneration of skeletal muscle, mostly due to a genetic disorder. Tetany: rapid spasms (wild contractions) in muscle due to low Ca⁺⁺ in body fluid. Arthritis: inflammation of joints. Osteoporosis: age-related disorder characterised by decreased bone mass and increased chances of fractures; decreased levels of oestrogen is a common cause. Gout: inflammation of joints due to accumulation of uric acid crystals. The skeletal system consists of 206 bones and a few cartilages; it is grouped into two principal divisions — the axial and the appendicular skeleton. The axial skeleton comprises 80 bones distributed along the main axis of the body; the skull, vertebral column, sternum and ribs constitute the axial skeleton. The skull is composed of two sets of bones — cranial and facial — that total 22 bones; a single U-shaped bone called hyoid is present at the base of the buccal cavity, and it is also included in the skull; each middle ear contains three tiny bones — malleus, incus and stapes — collectively called ear ossicles. The vertebral column is formed by 26 serially arranged units called vertebrae; there are 12 pairs of ribs.
Given: Six disorders; axial skeleton parts.
Formula/Principle: Classify by tissue and cause; sum bone counts.
Step 1: Joints: arthritis, gout ⇒ 2; autoimmune: myasthenia gravis ⇒ 1.
Step 2: Skull: 22 + 1 (hyoid) + 6 (ossicles) = 29.
Step 3: 29 + 26 + 1 + 24 = 80.
Why: Each disorder has a distinct site and cause — immune attack at the synapse, genetic degeneration, ion imbalance, inflammation, hormone-related bone loss or crystal deposition.
Why not the others: (A) Overcounts; 126 is the appendicular count. (B) Undercounts disorders. (D) 206 is the whole skeleton.
Key point: Myasthenia gravis autoimmune; arthritis and gout affect joints; axial skeleton 80 bones.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating net charge movement and ATP use by the sodium–potassium pump, and the structural types of neurons and their locations
questions.question: In a resting neuron, the Na⁺/K⁺ pump completes 200 cycles. How many Na⁺ ions leave, how many K⁺ ions enter, what net positive charge is moved out, and which statement about neuron types is correct?
options: A) 400 Na⁺ out, 600 K⁺ in; net charge moved in; bipolar neurons are found in the cerebral cortex

B) 600 Na⁺ out, 400 K⁺ in, net 200 positive charges out (one ATP per cycle, 200 ATP), making the inside more negative; multipolar neurons (one axon, two or more dendrites) are found in the cerebral cortex, bipolar neurons (one axon, one dendrite) in the retina, and unipolar neurons (cell body with one axon only) usually in the embryonic stage
C) 200 Na⁺ out, 200 K⁺ in; no net charge moved
D) 600 Na⁺ out, 400 K⁺ in; unipolar neurons are found in the retina
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 600 Na⁺ out, 400 K⁺ in, net 200 positive charges out; multipolar in cortex, bipolar in retina, unipolar in embryo.
Concept: Ionic gradients across the resting membrane are maintained by the active transport of ions by the sodium–potassium pump, which transports 3 Na⁺ outwards for 2 K⁺ into the cell; as a result, the outer surface of the axonal membrane possesses a positive charge while its inner surface becomes negatively charged and therefore is polarised; the electrical potential difference across the resting plasma membrane is called the resting potential. In the resting state the axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to potassium ions and nearly impermeable to sodium ions. A neuron is a microscopic structure composed of three major parts, namely the cell body, dendrites and axon. Based on the number of axons and dendrites, neurons are divided into three types: multipolar (with one axon and two or more dendrites; found in the cerebral cortex), bipolar (with one axon and one dendrite; found in the retina of the eye) and unipolar (cell body with one axon only; found usually in the embryonic stage).
Given: 200 pump cycles; 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per cycle.
Formula/Principle: Totals = cycles × ions per cycle; net charge = Na⁺ out − K⁺ in.
Step 1: Na⁺ out = 200 × 3 = 600.
Step 2: K⁺ in = 200 × 2 = 400.
Step 3: Net = 600 − 400 = 200 positive charges out; ATP = 200.
Why: The unequal exchange makes the pump electrogenic, adding to the negativity inside the membrane.
Why not the others: (A) Ratio reversed; cortex has multipolar neurons. (C) The pump is not 1 : 1. (D) The retina has bipolar neurons.
Key point: Na⁺/K⁺ pump: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP; multipolar (cortex), bipolar (retina), unipolar (embryo).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting observations on users of different contraceptive methods in terms of their mode of action, and the legal and medical basis of MTP
questions.question: In a family-welfare survey: woman W1 with a copper IUD has normal ovulation but no pregnancy; W2 takes a weekly non-steroidal pill; W3 took a pill within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse and did not become pregnant; W4 seeks termination of a 10-week pregnancy. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The copper IUD works by stopping ovulation; Saheli is a daily steroidal pill; MTP is allowed only after 24 weeks
B) W3's pill acts only as a barrier; MTP is safest in the third trimester
C) The copper IUD blocks the oviduct surgically; emergency pills must be taken before intercourse

D) Copper-releasing IUDs suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity and make the uterus unsuitable for implantation, so ovulation can continue; W2 is using Saheli, a once-a-week non-steroidal pill; W3 used emergency contraception, effective if progestogens or progestogen–oestrogen combinations or an IUD are used within 72 hours of coitus; W4's MTP falls in the first trimester (up to 12 weeks), when it is relatively safe, and MTP was legalised in India in 1971 with conditions to prevent its misuse
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Copper IUD acts on sperm and implantation; Saheli weekly non-steroidal pill; emergency contraception within 72 h; first-trimester MTP relatively safe; legalised 1971.
Concept: Intra uterine devices (IUDs) are inserted by doctors or expert nurses in the uterus through the vagina; these are presently available as the non-medicated IUDs (e.g. Lippes loop), copper releasing IUDs (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375) and the hormone releasing IUDs (Progestasert, LNG-20). IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperms within the uterus, and the Cu ions released suppress sperm motility and the fertilising capacity of sperms; the hormone releasing IUDs, in addition, make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to the sperms. Oral administration of small doses of either progestogens or progestogen–oestrogen combinations is another contraceptive method used by females; they are used in the form of tablets and hence are popularly called the pills; pills have to be taken daily for a period of 21 days starting preferably within the first five days of the menstrual cycle; they inhibit ovulation and implantation as well as alter the quality of cervical mucus to prevent or retard entry of sperms. Saheli, the new oral contraceptive for females, contains a non-steroidal preparation; it is a 'once a week' pill with very few side effects and high contraceptive value. Administration of progestogens or progestogen–oestrogen combinations or IUDs within 72 hours of coitus have been found to be very effective as emergency contraceptives, as they could be used to avoid possible pregnancy due to rape or casual unprotected intercourse. Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term is called medical termination of pregnancy (MTP) or induced abortion; the Government of India legalised MTP in 1971 with some strict conditions to avoid its misuse; MTPs are considered relatively safe during the first trimester, i.e. up to 12 weeks of pregnancy.
Step 1: W1: ovulation normal but no pregnancy ⇒ method acts after ovulation (sperm and implantation).
Step 2: W2: weekly non-steroidal pill ⇒ Saheli; W3: within 72 h ⇒ emergency contraception.
Step 3: W4: 10 weeks ⇒ first trimester ⇒ relatively safe MTP.
Why: Each observation points to the stage at which the method intervenes — gamete function, implantation or ovulation.
Why not the others: (A) IUDs do not stop ovulation; Saheli is weekly and non-steroidal; MTP timing wrong. (B) Emergency pills are hormonal; MTP is safest early. (C) IUDs are not surgical; emergency pills are taken after coitus.
Key point: Cu-IUD: ↓ sperm motility; Saheli weekly; emergency within 72 h; MTP safe up to 12 weeks.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading a table of chromosome numbers and sex chromosomes to identify XX–XY, ZW–ZZ, XO and haplodiploid sex determination
questions.question:
A table records chromosome data.

Organism | Female | Male
Human | 44 + XX | 44 + XY
Bird (fowl) | ZW | ZZ
Grasshopper | XX | XO (one fewer chromosome than female)
Honey bee | 32 (diploid, from fertilised egg) | 16 (haploid, from unfertilised egg)

Which interpretation of the table is correct?
options: A) In birds the male is heterogametic, producing two types of sperm
B) In humans, birds, grasshoppers and honey bees, the father always decides the sex of the offspring
C) Honey bee males have a father but no grandfather

D) In humans and grasshoppers the male is heterogametic (X and Y, or X and no X, sperm), so the father's sperm decides the sex; in birds the female (ZW) is heterogametic and the egg decides; in honey bees an unfertilised egg develops by parthenogenesis into a haploid male (drone) and a fertilised egg into a diploid female (queen or worker), so males produce sperm by mitosis, have no father and thus cannot have sons, but have a grandfather
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Male heterogamety in humans and grasshoppers; female heterogamety in birds; haplodiploidy in honey bees.
Concept: In a number of insects including the grasshopper, the XO type of sex determination is seen, in which all eggs bear an additional X chromosome besides the autosomes; some sperms bear the X chromosome whereas some do not; eggs fertilised by sperm having an X chromosome become females, and those fertilised by sperms that do not have an X chromosome become males. In many other insects and in mammals including man, XY type of sex determination is seen, where both male and female have the same number of chromosomes; males have an X and a Y chromosome along with autosomes, whereas females have a pair of X chromosomes. In both these cases males produce two different types of gametes, (a) either with or without the X chromosome or (b) some gametes with the X chromosome and some with the Y chromosome; such types of sex determination mechanisms are designated as examples of male heterogamety. In some other organisms, e.g. birds, a different mechanism of sex determination is observed: the total number of chromosomes is the same in both males and females, but two different types of gametes in terms of the sex chromosomes are produced by females, i.e. female heterogamety; to distinguish it, the two sex chromosomes of females are denoted Z and W, whereas males have a pair of Z chromosomes besides the autosomes. The sex determination in honey bee is based on the number of sets of chromosomes an individual receives: an offspring formed from the union of a sperm and an egg develops as a female (queen or worker), and an unfertilised egg develops as a male (drone) by means of parthenogenesis; this means that the males have half the number of chromosomes than that of females; the females are diploid having 32 chromosomes and males are haploid, i.e. having 16 chromosomes; this is called the haplodiploid sex-determination system and has special characteristic features such as the males produce sperms by mitosis, they do not have a father and thus cannot have sons, but have a grandfather and can have grandsons.
Given: Table of sex chromosome constitution.
Step 1: Human and grasshopper males produce two kinds of sperm ⇒ male heterogamety.
Step 2: Bird females (ZW) produce two kinds of eggs ⇒ female heterogamety.
Step 3: Honey bee sex depends on ploidy: haploid drone, diploid female.
Why: Whichever sex makes two kinds of gametes decides the sex of the progeny; in bees fertilisation itself decides.
Why not the others: (A) Bird males are ZZ (homogametic). (B) In birds the mother decides; in bees fertilisation decides. (C) Drones have no father but do have a maternal grandfather.
Key point: XY/XO: male heterogamety; ZW: female heterogamety; bees: haplodiploidy.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading codon assignments to predict the effect of point mutations and frameshifts, and the general properties of the genetic code
questions.question: Part of a codon table: GAG = Glu, GUG = Val, AUG = Met (start), UAA/UAG/UGA = stop. The mRNA 5′ AUG GAG … 3′ in the β-globin gene is changed to AUG GUG …; in a second mutant one base is inserted after AUG. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The first change replaces glutamic acid by valine (single base substitution A→U in the codon), as in sickle-cell anaemia; the insertion shifts the reading frame so all following codons are read differently (frameshift); the code is triplet and degenerate (61 codons for 20 amino acids, 3 stop codons), unambiguous, nearly universal, and read without punctuation, with AUG also coding for methionine
B) The first change is a frameshift, and the insertion is a point mutation that changes only one amino acid
C) Since the code is degenerate, any base change leaves the protein unchanged
D) There are 64 codons that each code for an amino acid; stop codons code for glycine
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) GAG → GUG gives Glu → Val (point mutation, sickle-cell); insertion is a frameshift; code triplet, degenerate, unambiguous, nearly universal, comma-less.
Concept: The salient features of the genetic code are as follows: (i) the codon is triplet; 61 codons code for amino acids and 3 codons do not code for any amino acids, hence they function as stop codons; (ii) one codon codes for only one amino acid, hence it is unambiguous and specific; (iii) some amino acids are coded by more than one codon, hence the code is degenerate; (iv) the codon is read in mRNA in a contiguous fashion; there are no punctuations; (v) the code is nearly universal: for example, from bacteria to human UUU would code for phenylalanine (Phe); some exceptions to this rule have been found in mitochondrial codons and in some protozoans; (vi) AUG has dual functions: it codes for methionine (met), and it also acts as an initiator codon. The relationship between genes and DNA is best understood by mutation studies; the effects of large deletions and rearrangements in a segment of DNA are easy to comprehend. A classical example of point mutation is a change of single base pair in the gene for beta globin chain that results in the change of amino acid residue glutamate to valine; it results in a diseased condition called sickle cell anaemia. Insertion or deletion of one or two bases changes the reading frame from the point of insertion or deletion; such mutations are referred to as frameshift insertion or deletion mutations; insertion or deletion of three or its multiple bases inserts or deletes one or multiple codons, hence one or multiple amino acids, and the reading frame remains unaltered from that point onwards.
Given: GAG → GUG; one-base insertion after AUG.
Step 1: GAG (Glu) → GUG (Val): single substitution ⇒ one amino acid changed.
Step 2: Insertion of one base ⇒ every downstream triplet regrouped ⇒ frameshift.
Step 3: Insertion of 3 bases would add one codon without shifting the frame.
Why: Because codons are read as non-overlapping triplets without gaps, a single insertion disturbs every codon after it.
Why not the others: (B) Types reversed. (C) Degeneracy does not protect every change; GAG → GUG alters the amino acid. (D) Only 61 codons code for amino acids; stop codons code for none.
Key point: Substitution → one amino acid may change (sickle-cell); insertion/deletion of 1–2 bases → frameshift.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting Fleming's observation of a mould inhibiting bacterial growth, and the later development and significance of penicillin and other antibiotics
questions.question: While culturing Staphylococcus, a scientist notices that the bacteria fail to grow in a zone around a contaminating mould. Which interpretation and follow-up are correct?
options: A) The mould consumed all the nutrients, so no chemical is involved

B) This was Alexander Fleming's observation; the mould Penicillium notatum released a chemical, named penicillin, that kills or retards the growth of bacteria; its full potential as an effective antibiotic was established later by Ernest Chain and Howard Florey, and penicillin was used extensively to treat wounded soldiers in World War II; antibiotics (anti = against, bio = life) produced by microbes kill or retard disease-causing microbes and have helped treat diseases such as plague, whooping cough, diphtheria and leprosy
C) The zone shows that the bacteria produced an antibiotic that killed the mould
D) Penicillin was discovered from a bacterium and acts mainly against viruses
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Fleming's observation of Penicillium notatum; penicillin; developed by Chain and Florey; used in WWII; antibiotics treat many bacterial diseases.
Concept: Antibiotics produced by microbes are regarded as one of the most significant discoveries of the twentieth century and have greatly contributed towards the welfare of human society; anti is a Greek word that means 'against', and bio means 'life'; together they mean 'against life' (in the context of disease-causing organisms), whereas with reference to human beings they are 'pro life' and not against. Antibiotics are chemical substances which are produced by some microbes and can kill or retard the growth of other (disease-causing) microbes. Penicillin was the first antibiotic to be discovered, and it was a chance discovery: Alexander Fleming, while working on Staphylococci bacteria, once observed a mould growing in one of his unwashed culture plates around which Staphylococci could not grow; he found out that it was due to a chemical produced by the mould and he named it penicillin after the mould Penicillium notatum. However, its full potential as an effective antibiotic was established much later by Ernest Chain and Howard Florey; this antibiotic was extensively used to treat American soldiers wounded in World War II; Fleming, Chain and Florey were awarded the Nobel Prize in 1945 for this discovery. After penicillin, other antibiotics were also purified from other microbes; antibiotics have greatly improved our capacity to treat deadly diseases such as plague, whooping cough (kali khansi), diphtheria (gal ghotu) and leprosy (kusht rog), which used to kill millions all over the globe.
Step 1: Clear zone around mould ⇒ diffusing inhibitory substance.
Step 2: Mould identified as Penicillium notatum ⇒ substance named penicillin.
Step 3: Purification and testing (Chain, Florey) ⇒ clinical antibiotic.
Why: A zone of inhibition centred on the mould shows a chemical spreading from it, not mere competition at the contact edge.
Why not the others: (A) Nutrient depletion would not produce a sharp clear zone around a small colony. (C) The bacteria were inhibited, not the mould. (D) Penicillin comes from a fungus and acts on bacteria.
Key point: Penicillin from Penicillium notatum (Fleming); developed by Chain and Florey; antibiotics act against bacteria.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the number of DNA copies after a given number of PCR cycles, the role of each step and of Taq polymerase, and PCR in early diagnosis
questions.question: A blood sample contains only 10 copies of an HIV DNA sequence. After 20 cycles of PCR with perfect doubling, about how many copies are present, and which statement about PCR is correct?
options: A) about 10⁷ copies (10 × 2²⁰ ≈ 1.05 × 10⁷); each cycle has denaturation of the double-stranded DNA at high temperature, annealing of two primers, and extension by thermostable Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus; because so few copies can be amplified, PCR detects very low concentrations of a pathogen in suspected AIDS or cancer patients before symptoms appear
B) 200 copies; Taq polymerase is used because it is active at low temperature
C) 2 × 10⁶ copies; primers are long RNA molecules that are not required in later cycles
D) 10 × 20² = 4000 copies; denaturation is done by enzymes at 37 °C
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) ≈ 1.05 × 10⁷ copies; denaturation, annealing, extension with Taq polymerase; early diagnosis.
Concept: PCR stands for polymerase chain reaction; in this reaction, multiple copies of the gene (or DNA) of interest are synthesised in vitro using two sets of primers (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides that are complementary to the regions of DNA) and the enzyme DNA polymerase. The enzyme extends the primers using the nucleotides provided in the reaction and the genomic DNA as template; if the process of replication of DNA is repeated many times, the segment of DNA can be amplified to approximately a billion times, i.e. 1 billion copies are made. Such repeated amplification is achieved by the use of a thermostable DNA polymerase (isolated from a bacterium, Thermus aquaticus), which remains active during the high temperature induced denaturation of double stranded DNA. Each cycle consists of denaturation, annealing of primers and extension. Using conventional methods of diagnosis (serum and urine analysis, etc.) early detection is not possible; recombinant DNA technology, PCR and ELISA are some of the techniques that serve the purpose of early diagnosis; presence of a pathogen is normally suspected only when the pathogen has produced a disease symptom, by which time the concentration of pathogen is already very high in the body; however, very low concentration of a bacteria or virus (at a time when the symptoms of the disease are not yet visible) can be detected by amplification of their nucleic acid by PCR; PCR is now routinely used to detect HIV in suspected AIDS patients and to detect mutations in genes in suspected cancer patients too.
Given: N₀ = 10, n = 20 cycles, perfect doubling.
Formula/Principle: N = N₀ × 2ⁿ.
Step 1: 2²⁰ = 1 048 576.
Step 2: N = 10 × 1 048 576 ≈ 1.05 × 10⁷.
Step 3: About 30 cycles from one copy gives 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹, the "billion copies" of PCR.
Why: Each cycle doubles the target, so amplification grows exponentially with the number of cycles.
Why not the others: (B) Linear growth; Taq is valued for heat stability. (C) Wrong number; primers are short DNA oligonucleotides used every cycle. (D) Wrong formula; denaturation is by heat.
Key point: PCR: N = N₀·2ⁿ; denature → anneal → extend (Taq); early detection of pathogens.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Ordering the steps in the fig–wasp mutualism and the sexual deceit of Ophrys, and distinguishing mutualism from commensalism with examples
questions.question: Which sequence and classification of interspecific interactions is correct?
options: A) In the fig–wasp relationship, the wasp feeds on fig fruits but gives nothing in return, so it is commensalism; barnacles on a whale harm the whale (parasitism)

B) The female fig wasp pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for egg-laying sites → she lays eggs in the fruit → the developing seeds feed the wasp larvae, a tightly linked one-to-one mutualism; the orchid Ophrys has a petal resembling the female bee, so the male bee 'pseudocopulates' and carries pollen to another flower; in commensalism one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited, as with an orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch, barnacles on a whale, the cattle egret feeding near grazing cattle, and clown fish among the tentacles of a sea anemone
C) Ophrys rewards the bee with nectar, so the relationship is commensalism
D) The cattle egret and cattle is an example of predation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Fig wasp pollinates while laying eggs; seeds feed larvae (mutualism); Ophrys sexual deceit; commensalism examples as listed.
Concept: Mutualism is an interaction that confers benefits on both the interacting species; lichens represent an intimate mutualistic relationship between a fungus and photosynthesising algae or cyanobacteria; similarly, the mycorrhizae are associations between fungi and the roots of higher plants. The most spectacular and evolutionarily fascinating examples of mutualism are found in plant–animal relationships: plants need the help of animals for pollinating their flowers and dispersing their seeds. In many species of fig trees there is a tight one-to-one relationship with the pollinator species of wasp; a given fig species can be pollinated only by its 'partner' wasp species and no other species; the female wasp uses the fruit not only as an oviposition (egg-laying) site but uses the developing seeds within the fruit for nourishing its larvae; the wasp pollinates the fig inflorescence while searching for suitable egg-laying sites; in return for the favour of pollination the fig offers the wasp some of its developing seeds as food for the developing wasp larvae. The Mediterranean orchid Ophrys employs 'sexual deceit' to get pollination done by a species of bee: one petal of its flower bears an uncanny resemblance to the female of the bee in size, colour and markings; the male bee is attracted to what it perceives as a female, 'pseudocopulates' with the flower, and during that process is dusted with pollen from the flower; when this same bee 'pseudocopulates' with another flower, it transfers pollen to it and thus pollinates the flower. Commensalism is the interaction in which one species benefits and the other is neither harmed nor benefited; an orchid growing as an epiphyte on a mango branch, and barnacles growing on the back of a whale, benefit while neither the mango tree nor the whale derives any apparent benefit; the cattle egret and grazing cattle in close association are a classic example of commensalism — the egrets always forage close to where the cattle are grazing because the cattle, as they move, stir up and flush out insects from the vegetation that otherwise might be difficult for the egrets to find and catch; another example is the interaction between sea anemone, which has stinging tentacles, and the clown fish that lives among them: the fish gets protection from predators, which stay away from the stinging tentacles, while the anemone does not appear to derive any benefit by hosting the clown fish.
Step 1: Wasp enters inflorescence → pollinates while searching for egg sites.
Step 2: Eggs laid → developing seeds nourish larvae → both partners benefit.
Step 3: Ophrys: male bee deceived → pollen carried to another flower.
Why: Mutualism benefits both partners; in commensalism only one gains, and the host is unaffected.
Why not the others: (A) Fig–wasp is mutualism; barnacles do not harm the whale. (C) Ophrys gives no reward; it deceives. (D) The egret does not prey on cattle.
Key point: Fig–wasp mutualism; Ophrys sexual deceit; commensalism: egret–cattle, clown fish–anemone, epiphytic orchid.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the effects of changes in an ecosystem's components — removing decomposers, shading the producers, or adding nutrients — using the structure and functions of a pond ecosystem
questions.question: In a small pond, (i) a chemical kills most bacteria and fungi in the sediment, (ii) floating weeds cover the surface and shade the water, (iii) runoff adds plenty of nitrate and phosphate. Which predicted effect is correct?
options: A) Killing decomposers would speed up nutrient release, because dead matter would no longer be locked up
B) Shading would raise primary productivity by lowering water temperature

C) Without decomposers, detritus would accumulate and inorganic nutrients would no longer be released from it, slowing mineral cycling; surface shading reduces light reaching phytoplankton and submerged plants, lowering gross primary productivity of the pond; added nitrate and phosphate first increase growth of algae (nutrients are limiting), as the pond is a self-sustaining unit in which abiotic components (water, soil, nutrients, light) and biotic components (producers, consumers, decomposers) interact through productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling
D) None of these changes affect the pond, because ecosystems are closed to the outside
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Detritus accumulates and nutrient release slows; shading lowers GPP; added nutrients boost algal growth.
Concept: An ecosystem can be visualised as a functional unit of nature, where living organisms interact among themselves and also with the surrounding physical environment. Let us take a pond as an example: this is fairly a self-sustainable unit and rather simple example that explains even the complex interactions that exist in an aquatic ecosystem; a pond is a shallow water body in which all the above-mentioned four basic components of an ecosystem are well exhibited; the abiotic component is the water with all the dissolved inorganic and organic substances and the rich soil deposit at the bottom of the pond; the solar input, the cycle of temperature, day-length and other climatic conditions regulate the rate of function of the entire pond; the autotrophic components include the phytoplankton, some algae and the floating, submerged and marginal plants found at the edges; the consumers are represented by the zooplankton, the free swimming and bottom dwelling forms; the decomposers are the fungi, bacteria and flagellates especially abundant in the bottom of the pond. This system performs all the functions of any ecosystem and of the biosphere as a whole, i.e. conversion of inorganic into organic material with the help of the radiant energy of the sun by the autotrophs; consumption of the autotrophs by heterotrophs; decomposition and mineralisation of the dead organic matter to release them back for reuse by the autotrophs. The important components of the ecosystem are productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling. Decomposers break down complex organic matter into inorganic substances like carbon dioxide, water and nutrients, and the process is called decomposition.
Step 1: Decomposers removed ⇒ mineralisation stops ⇒ detritus piles up, nutrients locked.
Step 2: Light reduced ⇒ photosynthesis of producers falls ⇒ GPP falls.
Step 3: N and P added ⇒ limiting nutrients relieved ⇒ algal growth increases.
Why: Each component performs a function — decomposers recycle nutrients, producers capture light — so removing or changing one alters the whole system.
Why not the others: (A) Decomposers are what release nutrients. (B) Less light lowers productivity. (D) Ecosystems exchange energy and matter with surroundings.
Key point: Ecosystem functions: productivity, decomposition, energy flow, nutrient cycling.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating India's share of global biodiversity relative to its land area, and the proportions of described animal and plant species
questions.question: India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area but about 8.1 per cent of global species diversity. Of all recorded species, more than 70 per cent are animals and plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) make up no more than 22 per cent. How many times is India's share of species greater than its share of land, and which statement is correct?
options: A) about 3.4 times; India is one of the 12 mega diversity countries, and among animals insects are the most species-rich group, making up more than 70 per cent of all animals, so out of every 10 animals on the planet 7 are insects
B) about 8.1 times; insects make up 22 per cent of animals
C) about 0.3 times; plants outnumber animals in recorded species
D) about 5.7 times; India has the highest number of described species of any country
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 8.1/2.4 ≈ 3.4 times; India is a mega diversity country; insects > 70 % of animals.
Concept: India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area, but its share of the global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent; that is what makes our country one of the 12 mega diversity countries of the world. Nearly 45,000 species of plants and twice as many of animals have been recorded from India. If we accept May's global estimates, only 22 per cent of the total species have been recorded so far; applying this proportion to India's diversity figures, we estimate that there are probably more than 1,00,000 plant species and more than 3,00,000 animal species yet to be discovered and described. Of all the species recorded, more than 70 per cent are animals, while plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) comprise no more than 22 per cent of the total; among animals, insects are the most species-rich taxonomic group, making up more than 70 per cent of the total; that means, out of every 10 animals on this planet, 7 are insects.
Given: India: 2.4 % land, 8.1 % species; animals > 70 %, insects > 70 % of animals.
Formula/Principle: Relative richness = share of species ÷ share of land.
Step 1: 8.1/2.4 = 3.375 ≈ 3.4.
Step 2: Insects among all species ≈ 0.7 × 0.7 ≈ 0.49 ⇒ about half of all recorded species.
Step 3: Insects among animals 70 % ⇒ 7 of every 10 animals.
Why: India's range of latitudes and habitats packs a disproportionate share of species into a small area.
Why not the others: (B) Uses only the species share; insects are > 70 %. (C) Ratio inverted; animals outnumber plants. (D) Wrong ratio and claim.
Key point: India: 2.4 % land, 8.1 % species (≈3.4×); insects > 70 % of animals.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the nature and composition of lichens, viruses and viroids, and why viruses are not placed in any of the five kingdoms
questions.question: Which explanation about lichens, viruses and viroids is correct?
options: A) Viruses are placed in Monera because they lack a nucleus
B) Lichens are a single organism formed by a fungus alone
C) Viroids have a protein coat but no nucleic acid

D) Lichens are symbiotic associations of algae (phycobiont, which prepares food) and fungi (mycobiont, which provides shelter and absorbs mineral nutrients and water), so closely linked that they appear as one organism, and they do not grow in polluted areas, making them good pollution indicators; viruses are inert crystalline structures outside the living cell, with a protein coat (capsid) around either RNA or DNA, and become active only inside a host, so they are not included in the five kingdoms; viroids, discovered by T.O. Diener as the cause of potato spindle tuber disease, are free RNA with no protein coat and of low molecular weight
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Lichens: alga + fungus mutualism, pollution indicators; viruses: nucleoprotein, active only in hosts, not in five kingdoms; viroids: free RNA, no coat.
Concept: In the five kingdom classification of Whittaker there is no mention of lichens and some acellular organisms like viruses, viroids and prions. Viruses did not find a place in classification since they are not considered truly 'living', if we understand living as those organisms that have a cell structure; the viruses are non-cellular organisms that are characterised by having an inert crystalline structure outside the living cell; once they infect a cell they take over the machinery of the host cell to replicate themselves, killing the host. The name virus, which means venom or poisonous fluid, was given by Dmitri Ivanowsky (1892), who recognised certain microbes as causal organisms of the mosaic disease of tobacco; M.W. Beijerinck (1898) called the fluid 'Contagium vivum fluidum' (infectious living fluid); W.M. Stanley (1935) showed that viruses could be crystallised and that crystals consist largely of proteins. In addition to proteins, viruses also contain genetic material, which could be either RNA or DNA; no virus contains both RNA and DNA; a virus is a nucleoprotein and the genetic material is infectious. In 1971, T.O. Diener discovered a new infectious agent that was smaller than viruses and caused potato spindle tuber disease; it was found to be a free RNA; it lacked the protein coat that is found in viruses, hence the name viroid; the RNA of the viroid was of low molecular weight. Lichens are symbiotic associations, i.e. mutually useful associations, between algae and fungi; the algal component is known as phycobiont and the fungal component as mycobiont, which are autotrophic and heterotrophic, respectively; algae prepare food for fungi and fungi provide shelter and absorb mineral nutrients and water for its partner; so close is their association that if one saw a lichen in nature one would never imagine that they had two different organisms within them; lichens are very good pollution indicators — they do not grow in polluted areas.
Why: Viruses lack cell structure and independent metabolism, so they fit no cellular kingdom; lichens are two organisms functioning as one.
Why not the others: (A) Viruses are acellular and are not in Monera. (B) Lichens include an alga or cyanobacterium. (C) Viroids lack a protein coat.
Key point: Lichen = phycobiont + mycobiont; virus = nucleoprotein; viroid = naked RNA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Identifying the plant group of unknown specimens from features of their life cycle and structure, and comparing bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms
questions.question: Three specimens are examined: X has a dominant, free-living, thalloid or leafy gametophyte with a sporophyte attached to it; Y has a dominant sporophyte with true roots, stems, leaves and vascular tissue but no seeds, and some members produce two kinds of spores; Z bears seeds on open megasporophylls in cones, with no ovary. Which identification is correct?
options: A) X is a pteridophyte; Y is a bryophyte; Z is an angiosperm
B) X is a gymnosperm because its gametophyte is dominant

C) X is a bryophyte (needing water for the swimming antherozoids to reach the egg); Y is a pteridophyte, and heterospory, as in Selaginella and Salvinia, is a precursor to the seed habit; Z is a gymnosperm with naked ovules (e.g. Cycas, Pinus); angiosperms, unlike all three, have ovules enclosed in an ovary and show double fertilisation with triploid endosperm
D) Z is an angiosperm because it has cones
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) X bryophyte; Y pteridophyte (heterospory a precursor to seeds); Z gymnosperm (naked ovules); angiosperms have an ovary and double fertilisation.
Concept: Bryophytes are also called amphibians of the plant kingdom because these plants can live in soil but are dependent on water for sexual reproduction; the plant body of bryophytes is more differentiated than that of algae — it is thallus-like and prostrate or erect, and attached to the substratum by unicellular or multicellular rhizoids; the main plant body of the bryophyte is haploid and produces gametes, hence it is called a gametophyte; the sporophyte is not free-living but attached to the photosynthetic gametophyte and derives nourishment from it. In pteridophytes the main plant body is a sporophyte which is differentiated into true root, stem and leaves; these organs possess well-differentiated vascular tissues; although pteridophytes are commonly found in damp, shady places, water is needed for fertilisation. In a majority of the pteridophytes all the spores are of similar kinds; such plants are called homosporous; genera like Selaginella and Salvinia, which produce two kinds of spores, macro (large) and micro (small) spores, are known as heterosporous; the development of the zygotes into young embryos takes place within the female gametophytes, and this event is a precursor to the seed habit, considered an important step in evolution. The gymnosperms (gymnos: naked, sperma: seeds) are plants in which the ovules are not enclosed by any ovary wall and remain exposed, both before and after fertilisation; the seeds that develop post-fertilisation are not covered, i.e. are naked; gymnosperms include medium-sized trees or tall trees and shrubs. Unlike the gymnosperms where the ovules are naked, in the angiosperms or flowering plants the pollen grains and ovules are developed in specialised structures called flowers, and the seeds are enclosed in fruits; double fertilisation produces a diploid zygote and a triploid primary endosperm nucleus.
Why: The dominant generation, presence of vascular tissue, and whether ovules are naked or enclosed are the key features separating these groups.
Why not the others: (A) X and Y swapped; Z lacks an ovary. (B) Gymnosperms have a dominant sporophyte. (D) Angiosperms have flowers, and ovules enclosed in an ovary.
Key point: Bryophytes: gametophyte dominant; pteridophytes: vascular, no seeds; gymnosperms: naked ovules; angiosperms: ovary.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Building the floral formula of a member of Solanaceae in order from symmetry and sex to gynoecium, and its distinguishing floral and economic features
questions.question: A flower of Solanum (potato family) is bisexual and actinomorphic, with five united sepals, five united petals, five stamens attached to the petals, and a superior bicarpellary syncarpous ovary that is bilocular with a swollen placenta bearing many ovules. Which floral formula and statement are correct?
options: A) ⊕ ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₍₅₎ A₅ G̲₍₂₎ is wrong because the stamens are free from the petals
B) % ⚥ K₅ C₁₊₂₍₂₎ A₍₉₎₊₁ G̲₁, as in Fabaceae

C) ⊕ ⚥ K₍₅₎ C̑₍₅₎A₅ G̲₍₂₎ — written in order as symmetry, sex, calyx, corolla, androecium and gynoecium, with the arc joining corolla and androecium showing epipetalous stamens and the line under G showing a superior ovary; the placenta is swollen and obliquely placed (axile placentation); the family includes food plants (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, ashwagandha), fumigatory (tobacco) and ornamentals (petunia)
D) ⊕ ⚥ K₅ C₅ A∞ Ḡ₍₂₎, with an inferior ovary
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ⊕ ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₍₅₎ A₅ G̲₍₂₎ with epipetalous stamens; swollen oblique placenta; economic plants as listed.
Concept: Floral formula is represented by some symbols: Br stands for bracteate, K stands for calyx, C for corolla, P for perianth, A for androecium and G for gynoecium, G̲ for superior ovary and Ḡ for inferior ovary, ♂ for male, ♀ for female, ⚥ for bisexual plants, ⊕ for actinomorphic and % for zygomorphic nature of flower; fusion is indicated by enclosing the figure within brackets, and adhesion by a line drawn above the symbols of the floral parts. Solanaceae is a large family, commonly called the 'potato family'; it is widely distributed in tropics, subtropics and even temperate zones. Floral characters: inflorescence solitary, axillary or cymose as in Solanum; flower bisexual, actinomorphic; calyx sepals five, united, persistent, valvate aestivation; corolla petals five, united, valvate aestivation; androecium stamens five, epipetalous; gynoecium bicarpellary, obliquely placed, syncarpous; ovary superior, bilocular, placenta swollen with many ovules, axile; fruits berry or capsule; seeds many, endospermous. Economic importance: many plants belonging to this family are sources of food (tomato, brinjal, potato), spice (chilli), medicine (belladonna, ashwagandha), fumigatory (tobacco) and ornamentals (petunia).
Step 1: Symmetry ⊕, sex ⚥.
Step 2: K₍₅₎ (united sepals), C₍₅₎ (united petals), A₅ joined to C (epipetalous).
Step 3: G̲₍₂₎: superior, bicarpellary, syncarpous.
Why: The fixed order of symbols lets any flower be summarised compactly and compared across families.
Why not the others: (A) The stamens are epipetalous, so this formula (without the arc) is incomplete, not wrong for the stated reason. (B) That is the Fabaceae formula. (D) Stamens are five and the ovary superior.
Key point: Solanaceae: ⊕ ⚥ K₍₅₎ C̑₍₅₎A₅ G̲₍₂₎; swollen oblique placenta.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Identifying dicot and monocot stems from transverse sections by the arrangement and type of vascular bundles, hypodermis and ground tissue
questions.question: Two stained transverse sections of young stems are compared. Section S1: vascular bundles arranged in a ring, each conjoint and open with cambium between xylem and phloem, collenchymatous hypodermis, endodermis rich in starch grains, and a large pith. Section S2: numerous vascular bundles scattered in the ground tissue, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, conjoint and closed, with water-containing cavities; sclerenchymatous hypodermis; no distinct pith. Which identification is correct?
options: A) S1 is a monocot stem and S2 a dicot stem
B) Both are roots, because they have vascular bundles
C) S2 can undergo secondary growth because its bundles are closed

D) S1 is a dicot stem (e.g. sunflower), its open bundles allowing secondary growth, with the endodermis also called the starch sheath; S2 is a monocot stem (e.g. maize), with scattered closed bundles lacking cambium, sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, phloem parenchyma absent and water-containing cavities present
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) S1 dicot stem (ring of open bundles, starch sheath, pith); S2 monocot stem (scattered closed bundles with sheath, water cavities).
Concept: The transverse section of a typical young dicotyledonous stem shows that the epidermis is the outermost protective layer of the stem, covered with a thin layer of cuticle; the cells arranged in multiple layers between epidermis and pericycle constitute the cortex, which consists of three sub-zones: the outer hypodermis, consisting of a few layers of collenchymatous cells just below the epidermis, which provide mechanical strength to the young stem; cortical layers below hypodermis consisting of rounded thin-walled parenchymatous cells with conspicuous intercellular spaces; the innermost layer of the cortex is called the endodermis; the cells of the endodermis are rich in starch grains and the layer is also referred to as the starch sheath. Pericycle is present on the inner side of the endodermis and above the phloem in the form of semi-lunar patches of sclerenchyma; a large number of vascular bundles are arranged in a ring; the 'ring' arrangement of vascular bundles is a characteristic of the dicot stem; each vascular bundle is conjoint, open, and with endarch protoxylem; a large number of rounded parenchymatous cells with large intercellular spaces which occupy the central portion of the stem constitute the pith. The monocot stem has a sclerenchymatous hypodermis, a large number of scattered vascular bundles, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath, and a large, conspicuous parenchymatous ground tissue; vascular bundles are conjoint and closed; peripheral vascular bundles are generally smaller than the centrally located ones; the phloem parenchyma is absent, and water-containing cavities are present within the vascular bundles.
Step 1: Ring of open bundles + collenchymatous hypodermis + pith ⇒ dicot stem.
Step 2: Scattered closed bundles with sheath + sclerenchymatous hypodermis + water cavities ⇒ monocot stem.
Step 3: Cambium in open bundles ⇒ secondary growth possible only in S1.
Why: The arrangement of bundles and the presence of cambium are the most reliable features for distinguishing stems of the two classes.
Why not the others: (A) Labels reversed. (B) Conjoint bundles and a hypodermis indicate stems; roots have radial bundles. (C) Closed bundles lack cambium.
Key point: Dicot stem: ring, open bundles; monocot stem: scattered, closed bundles with sheath.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The path of food through the alimentary canal of the frog and the switch between cutaneous and pulmonary respiration in water and on land
questions.question: Which sequence and description of digestion and respiration in the frog is correct?
options: A) Mouth → stomach → buccal cavity → oesophagus → intestine → cloaca; frogs breathe only through lungs

B) Food passes mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → intestine → rectum → cloaca; the frog catches prey with its bilobed tongue; bile from the gall bladder emulsifies fat and pancreatic juice digests carbohydrates and proteins in the duodenum, and digested food is absorbed by villi and microvilli of the intestine; in water the frog respires through its moist skin (cutaneous respiration) by diffusion, while on land the buccal cavity, skin and lungs serve as respiratory organs, and during aestivation and hibernation gaseous exchange takes place through the skin
C) The frog's alimentary canal is long because it is herbivorous; respiration in water is through gills in the adult
D) Pancreatic juice is secreted into the stomach; the frog breathes through lungs while submerged
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Mouth → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → intestine → rectum → cloaca; cutaneous respiration in water; skin, buccal cavity and lungs on land.
Concept: The digestive system of the frog consists of the alimentary canal and digestive glands; the alimentary canal is short because frogs are carnivores and hence the length of the intestine is reduced. The mouth opens into the buccal cavity that leads to the oesophagus through the pharynx; the oesophagus is a short tube that opens into the stomach, which in turn continues as the intestine, rectum and finally opens outside by the cloaca. The liver secretes bile that is stored in the gall bladder; the pancreas, a digestive gland, produces pancreatic juice containing digestive enzymes. Food is captured by the bilobed tongue; digestion of food takes place by the action of HCl and gastric juices secreted from the walls of the stomach; partially digested food called chyme is passed from the stomach to the first part of the intestine, the duodenum; the duodenum receives bile from the gall bladder and pancreatic juices from the pancreas through a common bile duct; bile emulsifies fat and pancreatic juices digest carbohydrates and proteins; final digestion takes place in the intestine; digested food is absorbed by the numerous finger-like folds in the inner wall of the intestine called villi and microvilli; the undigested solid waste moves into the rectum and passes out through the cloaca. Frogs respire on land and in the water by two different methods: in water, the skin acts as an aquatic respiratory organ (cutaneous respiration); dissolved oxygen in the water is exchanged through the skin by diffusion; on land, the buccal cavity, skin and lungs act as the respiratory organs; the respiration by lungs is called pulmonary respiration; the lungs are a pair of elongated, pink coloured sac-like structures present in the upper part of the trunk region (thorax); air enters through the nostrils into the buccal cavity and then to the lungs; during aestivation and hibernation gaseous exchange takes place through the skin.
Step 1: Ingestion with bilobed tongue → buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus.
Step 2: Stomach (HCl, gastric juice) → duodenum (bile, pancreatic juice) → intestine (absorption).
Step 3: Rectum → cloaca; respiration by skin in water, skin + buccal cavity + lungs on land.
Why: A short gut suits a carnivorous diet; a moist, vascular skin allows the frog to exchange gases both in water and during dormancy.
Why not the others: (A) Order wrong; skin also respires. (C) Frogs are carnivores with a short gut; adults lack gills. (D) Pancreatic juice enters the duodenum; underwater respiration is cutaneous.
Key point: Frog gut short (carnivore); cutaneous respiration in water and dormancy; pulmonary on land.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Predicting the effects of drugs or defects that act on ribosomes, mitochondria and plastids, using their structure and the presence of 70S ribosomes and DNA in organelles
questions.question: An antibiotic that blocks 70S ribosomes is found to affect protein synthesis in bacteria and, to a small extent, inside mitochondria of human cells, but not on the cytoplasmic ribosomes of human cells. A plant mutant cannot make chloroplasts but still forms colourless plastids that store starch. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain their own small circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, so a drug acting on 70S ribosomes can affect them, whereas eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S; leucoplasts are colourless plastids storing nutrients, amyloplasts storing starch; the mitochondrion's inner membrane forms cristae and its matrix is the site of aerobic respiration, while chloroplast thylakoids hold chlorophyll and the stroma contains enzymes for sugar synthesis
B) Mitochondria have 80S ribosomes like the cytoplasm, so the result must be an error
C) The mutant lacks all plastids, because amyloplasts are a type of chloroplast with chlorophyll
D) Ribosomes are membrane-bound organelles found only in eukaryotic cells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Organelles have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes; cytoplasm has 80S; leucoplasts/amyloplasts store starch; cristae, matrix, thylakoids and stroma as described.
Concept: Mitochondria (sing.: mitochondrion), unless specifically stained, are not easily visible under the microscope; the number of mitochondria per cell is variable depending on the physiological activity of the cells; each mitochondrion is a double membrane-bound structure with the outer membrane and the inner membrane dividing its lumen distinctly into two aqueous compartments, i.e. the outer compartment and the inner compartment; the inner compartment is called the matrix; the inner membrane forms a number of infoldings called the cristae towards the matrix; the cristae increase the surface area; mitochondria are the sites of aerobic respiration; the matrix also possesses a single circular DNA molecule, a few RNA molecules, ribosomes (70S) and the components required for the synthesis of proteins; the mitochondria divide by fission. Plastids are found in all plant cells and in euglenoides; based on the type of pigments, plastids can be classified into chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts; the leucoplasts are the colourless plastids of varied shapes and sizes with stored nutrients: amyloplasts store carbohydrates (starch), e.g. potato; elaioplasts store oils and fats; and the aleuroplasts store proteins. Within the stroma of the chloroplast, there are a number of organised flattened membranous sacs called the thylakoids; the stroma of the chloroplast contains enzymes required for the synthesis of carbohydrates and proteins; it also contains small, double-stranded circular DNA molecules and ribosomes; chlorophyll pigments are present in the thylakoids; the ribosomes of the chloroplasts are smaller (70S) than the cytoplasmic ribosomes (80S). Ribosomes are the granular structures first observed under the electron microscope as dense particles by George Palade (1953); they are composed of ribonucleic acid (RNA) and proteins and are not surrounded by any membrane; the eukaryotic ribosomes are 80S while the prokaryotic ribosomes are of 70S type; each ribosome has two subunits, larger and smaller subunits.
Step 1: Drug acts on 70S ⇒ bacteria and organelle ribosomes affected.
Step 2: Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S ⇒ unaffected.
Step 3: Colourless starch-storing plastids ⇒ amyloplasts (leucoplasts), which need no chlorophyll.
Why: The prokaryote-like ribosomes and DNA of mitochondria and chloroplasts make them semi-autonomous and sensitive to drugs that target bacterial ribosomes.
Why not the others: (B) Organelles have 70S ribosomes. (C) Amyloplasts are colourless leucoplasts. (D) Ribosomes are non-membranous and found in all cells.
Key point: Mitochondria and plastids: own DNA + 70S ribosomes; cytoplasm 80S; amyloplasts store starch.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing DNA content and chromosome number of a cell in G₁, S, G₂ and the stages of mitosis and meiosis
questions.question: A somatic cell in G₁ has DNA content 2C and chromosome number 2n. Which comparison of the cell cycle stages is correct?
options: A) DNA content doubles during G₂, and chromosome number doubles during S phase

B) During S phase DNA content rises from 2C to 4C while the chromosome number stays 2n (each chromosome now has two sister chromatids); G₂ cells have 4C and 2n; after mitosis each daughter cell has 2C and 2n; after meiosis I each cell has 2C and n, and after meiosis II each cell has 1C and n; quiescent cells that do not divide further leave G₁ to enter G₀
C) Chromosome number becomes 4n after S phase
D) Each cell after meiosis II has 2C and 2n
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) S: 2C → 4C, 2n unchanged; G₂ 4C, 2n; after mitosis 2C, 2n; after meiosis I 2C, n; after meiosis II 1C, n; G₀ exit from G₁.
Concept: The cell cycle is divided into two basic phases: interphase, a period of preparation for cell division, and the M phase (mitosis phase). The interphase is divided into three further phases: G₁ phase (Gap 1), S phase (Synthesis) and G₂ phase (Gap 2). G₁ phase corresponds to the interval between mitosis and initiation of DNA replication; during G₁ phase the cell is metabolically active and continuously grows but does not replicate its DNA. S or synthesis phase marks the period during which DNA synthesis or replication takes place; during this time the amount of DNA per cell doubles: if the initial amount of DNA is denoted as 2C then it increases to 4C; however, there is no increase in the chromosome number: if the cell had diploid or 2n number of chromosomes at G₁, even after S phase the number of chromosomes remains the same, i.e. 2n. During the G₂ phase, proteins are synthesised in preparation for mitosis while cell growth continues. Some cells in the adult animals do not appear to exhibit division (e.g. heart cells) and many other cells divide only occasionally; these cells that do not divide further exit G₁ phase to enter an inactive stage called quiescent stage (G₀) of the cell cycle. Meiosis involves two sequential cycles of nuclear and cell division called meiosis I and meiosis II but only a single cycle of DNA replication; meiosis I is initiated after the parental chromosomes have replicated to produce identical sister chromatids at the S phase; meiosis involves pairing of homologous chromosomes and recombination between non-sister chromatids; four haploid cells are formed at the end of meiosis II.
Step 1: G₁: 2C, 2n → S: 4C, 2n (sister chromatids joined at the centromere).
Step 2: Mitosis separates sister chromatids ⇒ each daughter 2C, 2n.
Step 3: Meiosis I separates homologues ⇒ 2C, n; meiosis II separates chromatids ⇒ 1C, n.
Why: Chromosome number is counted by centromeres, which do not double in S phase, whereas DNA amount does.
Why not the others: (A) DNA doubles in S, and chromosome number does not double there. (C) Number stays 2n. (D) Meiotic products are haploid with 1C.
Key point: S phase doubles DNA (2C → 4C) but not chromosome number.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading data on the rate of photosynthesis at different light intensities and CO₂ concentrations in terms of Blackman's law of limiting factors and the responses of C₃ and C₄ plants
questions.question:
Rates of photosynthesis (arbitrary units) of a C₃ plant were measured.

Light intensity | CO₂ 0.03 % | CO₂ 0.05 %
Low | 5 | 5
Medium | 12 | 15
High | 14 | 24
Very high | 14 | 24

Which interpretation of these data is correct?
options: A) At low light, CO₂ is the limiting factor, so raising CO₂ increases the rate
B) Light has no effect on photosynthesis once CO₂ is above 0.03 %
C) Raising CO₂ beyond 0.05 % would have no effect on any plant

D) According to Blackman's law, when several factors affect a process its rate is determined by the factor nearest to its minimal value; at low light, light is limiting, so extra CO₂ has no effect; at high light, the rate levels off at 14 with 0.03 % CO₂ because CO₂ becomes limiting, and rises to 24 with 0.05 % CO₂; light saturation occurs at about 10 per cent of full sunlight, so light is rarely limiting in nature except for shaded plants, while C₃ plants respond to higher CO₂ (up to about 450 μL L⁻¹), which is why greenhouse crops such as tomatoes and bell peppers are grown in CO₂-enriched air
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Blackman's law: light limiting at low intensity; CO₂ limiting at high intensity; C₃ plants benefit from CO₂ enrichment.
Concept: The rate of photosynthesis is very important in determining the yield of plants, including crop plants; photosynthesis is under the influence of several factors, both internal (plant) and external; the plant factors include the number, size, age and orientation of leaves, mesophyll cells and chloroplasts, internal CO₂ concentration and the amount of chlorophyll; the external factors would include the availability of sunlight, temperature, CO₂ concentration and water. Blackman's (1905) law of limiting factors states: if a chemical process is affected by more than one factor, then its rate will be determined by the factor which is nearest to its minimal value; it is the factor which directly affects the process if its quantity is changed. There is a linear relationship between incident light and CO₂ fixation rates at low light intensities; at higher light intensities, gradually the rate does not show further increase as other factors become limiting; light saturation occurs at 10 per cent of the full sunlight; hence, except for plants in shade or in dense forests, light is rarely a limiting factor in nature. Carbon dioxide is the major limiting factor for photosynthesis; the concentration of CO₂ is very low in the atmosphere (between 0.03 and 0.04 per cent); increase in concentration up to 0.05 per cent can cause an increase in CO₂ fixation rates; beyond this the levels can become damaging over longer periods. C₃ and C₄ plants respond differently to CO₂ concentrations: at low light conditions neither group responds to high CO₂ conditions; at high light intensities, both C₃ and C₄ plants show increase in the rates of photosynthesis; C₄ plants show saturation at about 360 μL L⁻¹, while C₃ plants respond to increased CO₂ concentration and saturation is seen only beyond 450 μL L⁻¹; thus current availability of CO₂ levels is limiting to the C₃ plants; the fact that C₃ plants respond to higher CO₂ concentration by showing increased rates of photosynthesis leading to higher productivity has been used for some greenhouse crops such as tomatoes and bell pepper.
Given: Table of rates.
Step 1: Low light: 5 at both CO₂ ⇒ light limiting.
Step 2: High light: 14 vs 24 ⇒ CO₂ limiting at 0.03 %.
Step 3: Very high light: no further rise ⇒ light no longer limiting.
Why: Only the factor in shortest supply controls the rate; improving any other factor has no effect until that one is relieved.
Why not the others: (A) At low light, light is limiting. (B) Light matters at low intensities. (C) C₃ plants respond up to about 450 μL L⁻¹, and high levels can be damaging over long periods, not "no effect for all plants".
Key point: Blackman's law: rate set by the factor nearest its minimum.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating net ATP and NADH from glycolysis and the products and energy yield of alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation
questions.question: Yeast cells ferment 10 molecules of glucose anaerobically. How many net ATP and how many CO₂ molecules are formed, and which statement is correct?
options: A) 20 net ATP and 20 CO₂ molecules (each glucose → 2 pyruvate → 2 ethanol + 2 CO₂); in glycolysis 4 ATP are made but 2 are used, and the 2 NADH formed are reoxidised to NAD⁺ when acetaldehyde is reduced to ethanol (or pyruvate to lactic acid in muscle), so no NADH is left; fermentation releases less than seven per cent of the energy in glucose, and yeast is poisoned when ethanol reaches about 13 per cent
B) 40 net ATP and 20 CO₂; NADH accumulates during fermentation
C) 20 net ATP and 0 CO₂; ethanol is formed directly from glucose without pyruvate
D) 380 net ATP and 60 CO₂
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 20 ATP and 20 CO₂; NADH reoxidised; < 7 % energy released; yeast tolerates about 13 % ethanol.
Concept: The scheme of glycolysis was given by Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and J. Parnas, and is often referred to as the EMP pathway; in anaerobic organisms it is the only process in respiration. In glycolysis, glucose undergoes partial oxidation to form two molecules of pyruvic acid; ATP is utilised at two steps — first in the conversion of glucose into glucose 6-phosphate and second in the conversion of fructose 6-phosphate to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate; two redox-equivalents are removed (in the form of two hydrogen atoms) from PGAL and transferred to NAD⁺ forming NADH + H⁺; the conversion of BPGA to 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA) is also an energy-yielding process, trapped by the formation of ATP; another ATP is synthesised during the conversion of PEP to pyruvic acid; four ATP are formed in all and two used, a net gain of 2 ATP. In fermentation, say by yeast, the incomplete oxidation of glucose is achieved under anaerobic conditions by sets of reactions where pyruvic acid is converted to CO₂ and ethanol; the enzymes pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase catalyse these reactions; other organisms like some bacteria produce lactic acid from pyruvic acid; in animal cells also, like muscles during exercise, when oxygen is inadequate for cellular respiration pyruvic acid is reduced to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase; the reducing agent is NADH + H⁺, which is reoxidised to NAD⁺ in both processes. In both lactic acid and alcohol fermentation not much energy is released; less than seven per cent of the energy in glucose is released and not all of it is trapped as high energy bonds of ATP; also, the processes are hazardous — either acid or alcohol is produced; yeasts poison themselves to death when the concentration of alcohol reaches about 13 per cent.
Given: 10 glucose; alcoholic fermentation.
Formula/Principle: Per glucose: net 2 ATP; 2 pyruvate → 2 ethanol + 2 CO₂.
Step 1: ATP = 10 × 2 = 20.
Step 2: CO₂ = 10 × 2 = 20.
Step 3: NADH from glycolysis (20) used to reduce 20 acetaldehyde ⇒ net NADH 0.
Why: Regenerating NAD⁺ is the purpose of fermentation; without it glycolysis would stop for lack of NAD⁺.
Why not the others: (B) Double counts ATP; NADH is reoxidised. (C) Fermentation releases CO₂ and passes through pyruvate. (D) Uses aerobic yields.
Key point: Glycolysis net 2 ATP; fermentation regenerates NAD⁺; yeast: ethanol + CO₂.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Finding the cell constant from a standard KCl solution and then the conductivity and molar conductivity of another solution from its resistance
questions.question: A conductivity cell filled with 0.1 M KCl (κ = 1.29 S m⁻¹) has resistance 100 Ω. Filled with a 0.05 M solution of an electrolyte, its resistance is 645 Ω. What are the cell constant, the conductivity and the molar conductivity of the second solution?
options: A) G* = 1.29 m⁻¹; κ = 0.002 S m⁻¹; Λm = 0.04 S cm² mol⁻¹
B) G* = 129 m⁻¹; κ = 0.20 S m⁻¹; Λm = 4 × 10⁻³ S m² mol⁻¹ = 40 S cm² mol⁻¹
C) G* = 129 m⁻¹; κ = 0.20 S m⁻¹; Λm = 4.0 S m² mol⁻¹
D) G* = 0.775 m⁻¹; κ = 500 S m⁻¹; Λm = 10⁴ S cm² mol⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) G* = 129 m⁻¹; κ = 0.20 S m⁻¹; Λm = 40 S cm² mol⁻¹.
Concept: The resistance of a conductor is R = ρ(l/A); the inverse of resistance is conductance, G = 1/R, and the inverse of resistivity is conductivity, κ = 1/ρ, so κ = G × (l/A). The quantity l/A is called the cell constant, denoted G*; it depends on the distance between the electrodes and their area of cross-section, and is determined by measuring the resistance of the cell containing a solution whose conductivity is already known — for this purpose, KCl solutions whose conductivity is known accurately at various concentrations and temperatures are generally used. Once the cell constant is known, the conductivity of any solution is κ = G*/R. It is more meaningful to compare conductivities per mole of electrolyte: the molar conductivity of a solution at a given concentration is the conductance of the volume V of solution containing one mole of electrolyte kept between two electrodes with area of cross-section A and distance of unit length; Λm = κ/c, and if κ is in S m⁻¹ and c in mol m⁻³, Λm is in S m² mol⁻¹; 1 S m² mol⁻¹ = 10⁴ S cm² mol⁻¹.
Given: κ(KCl) = 1.29 S m⁻¹, R(KCl) = 100 Ω; c = 0.05 M = 50 mol m⁻³, R = 645 Ω.
Formula/Principle: G* = κR; κ = G*/R; Λm = κ/c.
Step 1: G* = 1.29 × 100 = 129 m⁻¹.
Step 2: κ = 129/645 = 0.20 S m⁻¹.
Step 3: Λm = 0.20/50 = 4.0 × 10⁻³ S m² mol⁻¹ = 40 S cm² mol⁻¹.
Why: The cell constant is a property of the cell alone, so it can be found once with a standard and reused for any solution.
Why not the others: (A) Divides κ by R to get G*. (C) Uses c in mol L⁻¹ with κ in S m⁻¹. (D) Inverts the relation.
Key point: G* = κR (standard); κ = G*/R; Λm = κ/c (c in mol m⁻³).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Expressing the rate of a reaction in terms of each reactant and product, and distinguishing average rate over an interval from instantaneous rate at a moment
questions.question: For 2N₂O₅(g) → 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g), at a certain instant d[NO₂]/dt = 2.8 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. Which statement about the rates is correct?
options: A) −d[N₂O₅]/dt = 1.4 × 10⁻³ and d[O₂]/dt = 7.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, since rate = −½ d[N₂O₅]/dt = ¼ d[NO₂]/dt = d[O₂]/dt; the instantaneous rate is the slope of the tangent to the concentration–time curve at that instant, whereas the average rate, Δ[R]/Δt over an interval, approaches the instantaneous rate as Δt → 0; the rate is greatest at the start and falls as reactants are used up
B) All species change at the same rate, 2.8 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
C) −d[N₂O₅]/dt = 5.6 × 10⁻³ and d[O₂]/dt = 1.12 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹
D) The average rate over any interval always equals the instantaneous rate at its start
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) −d[N₂O₅]/dt = 1.4 × 10⁻³; d[O₂]/dt = 7.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; instantaneous rate = tangent slope.
Concept: The rate of a reaction can be defined as the change in concentration of a reactant or product in unit time; to be more specific, it can be expressed in terms of the rate of decrease in concentration of any one of the reactants or the rate of increase in concentration of any one of the products. The average rate depends upon the change in concentration of reactants or products and the time taken for that change to occur: r_av = −Δ[R]/Δt = Δ[P]/Δt. The rate of reaction at a particular moment of time is expressed as the instantaneous rate; it is obtained when we consider the average rate at the smallest time interval, say dt (i.e. when Δt approaches zero); it can be determined graphically by drawing a tangent at time t on either of the curves for concentration of R and P versus time and calculating its slope. When stoichiometric coefficients of reactants or products are not equal to one, the rate of disappearance of any of the reactants or the rate of appearance of products is divided by their respective stoichiometric coefficients so that a single value of rate is obtained for the reaction.
Given: d[NO₂]/dt = 2.8 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹; coefficients 2, 4, 1.
Formula/Principle: Rate = −½ d[N₂O₅]/dt = ¼ d[NO₂]/dt = d[O₂]/dt.
Step 1: Rate = 2.8 × 10⁻³/4 = 7.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹ = d[O₂]/dt.
Step 2: −d[N₂O₅]/dt = 2 × 7.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 1.4 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹.
Step 3: Instantaneous rate = slope of the tangent; average rate = chord slope over Δt.
Why: Dividing by stoichiometric coefficients gives one rate for the whole reaction, independent of which species is measured.
Why not the others: (B) Species change at rates in proportion to their coefficients. (C) Multiplies instead of dividing. (D) The rate falls with time, so a chord slope differs from the initial tangent slope.
Key point: Rate = −(1/a)d[A]/dt = (1/b)d[B]/dt; instantaneous rate = tangent slope.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Writing electronic configurations of 3d metals and their ions, counting unpaired electrons and spin-only moments, and relating the highest oxidation state to the number of 3d and 4s electrons
questions.question: For Cr, Mn²⁺, Fe²⁺, Cu²⁺ and Zn²⁺, which set of results is correct?
options: A) Cr: 3d⁴4s², 4 unpaired; Mn²⁺: 3d³; Zn²⁺ is paramagnetic

B) Cr: 3d⁵4s¹ with 6 unpaired electrons; Mn²⁺ 3d⁵, μ = 5.92 BM; Fe²⁺ 3d⁶, μ = 4.90 BM; Cu²⁺ 3d⁹, μ = 1.73 BM; Zn²⁺ 3d¹⁰ diamagnetic and colourless; manganese shows a maximum oxidation state of +7, equal to its total 3d + 4s electrons (5 + 2)
C) Fe²⁺: 3d⁴4s², μ = 4.90 BM; Mn shows a maximum of +2
D) Cu²⁺ has 3d¹⁰ and is diamagnetic; Cr has 4 unpaired electrons
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cr 3d⁵4s¹ (6 unpaired); Mn²⁺ 5.92, Fe²⁺ 4.90, Cu²⁺ 1.73 BM; Zn²⁺ diamagnetic; Mn up to +7.
Concept: The d-block elements have the general outer electronic configuration (n−1)d¹⁻¹⁰ns¹⁻²; however, there are exceptions due to very little energy difference between (n−1)d and ns orbitals; half and completely filled sets of orbitals are relatively more stable, and this factor is reflected in the configurations of Cr and Cu in the 3d series: Cr is 3d⁵4s¹ rather than 3d⁴4s², and Cu is 3d¹⁰4s¹. One of the notable features of transition elements is the great variety of oxidation states these may show in their compounds; the elements which give the greatest number of oxidation states occur in or near the middle of the series; manganese, for example, exhibits all the oxidation states from +2 to +7; the lesser number of oxidation states at the extreme ends stems from either too few electrons to lose or share (Sc, Ti) or too many d electrons (hence fewer orbitals available in which to share electrons with others) for higher valence (Cu, Zn). The magnetic moment is determined by the number of unpaired electrons and is calculated by using the 'spin-only' formula μ = √(n(n+2)) BM. When an electron from a lower energy d orbital is excited to a higher energy d orbital, the energy of excitation corresponds to the frequency of light absorbed; this frequency generally lies in the visible region, so most transition metal ions are coloured; ions with d⁰ or d¹⁰ configurations, such as Zn²⁺, are colourless.
Given: Z: Cr 24, Mn 25, Fe 26, Cu 29, Zn 30.
Formula/Principle: μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM; ions lose 4s electrons first.
Step 1: Cr [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ ⇒ 6 unpaired.
Step 2: Mn²⁺ d⁵ (n = 5): √35 = 5.92; Fe²⁺ d⁶ (n = 4): √24 = 4.90; Cu²⁺ d⁹ (n = 1): √3 = 1.73.
Step 3: Zn²⁺ d¹⁰ ⇒ n = 0; Mn maximum oxidation state = 5 + 2 = +7 (as in MnO₄⁻).
Why: Extra stability of a half-filled d⁵ set makes Cr adopt 3d⁵4s¹; magnetism and colour depend on unpaired d electrons.
